newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends above 7,500, bonds fall, dollar mixed.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends above 7,500, bonds fall, dollar mixed.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average roared past yet another milestone on Tuesday, closing above the 7,500-point level for the first time in its history.
Bonds fell as the market had little economic data to trade on. The dollar was mixed.

The Dow gained rose 60.77 to 7,539.27, the third straight record finish for blue chips. The broad market turned in a mixed performance, however, with stocks in technology and transportation companies slumping.
Advancers outpaced decliners 1,404 to 1,131 on heavy volume of almost 527 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the continuing rally among top-tier stocks reflects a market that remains awash in cash, although several noted the source of that cash appears to have changed.
In the past, mutual fund inflows have generally been cited as the key contributor to the stock market's relentless climb.
Analysts said the rally now appeared to be developing an international flavor amid mounting political and economic questions over the future of European Monetary Union (EMU).

"It seems like, suddenly, we have all these questions about whether EMU will be delayed or whether we will be facing a much-weakened European currency," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest.

"If you look at the stocks in the Dow that were up today, like Boeing and Caterpillar and Chevron, these are the kinds of internationally recognised names that foreign investors tend to buy," he said.

Shares in Boeing Co. gained 1-1/2 to 57-1/2 after the company announced it had signed several major aircraft sale contracts. Caterpillar Inc. gained 1-3/4 to 103-5/8 and Chevron Corp. rose 1-1/2 to 73-3/8.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 10.35 points to 1,401.69, snapping its three-session winning streak as several networking and semiconductor equipment stocks tumbled.

In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury fell 7/32, or $2.1875 on a $1,000 bond, pushing the yield up to 6.84 percent from 6.82 percent at Monday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The dollar fell as low as 111.85 yen in late trading ahead of an overnight report expected to show Japan's trade surplus grew yet again in April. The dollar quickly pared losses to end at 112.37 yen, below Monday's close of 112.95.
But the dollar rose to 1.7185 German marks from 1.7070, ending a two-day losing streak, as tensions eased over Europe's plan for a single currency.

In commodity markets, coffee prices fell to the lowest level in a month as weather forecasts calling for milder temperatures in Brazil sparked a rush to exit the market by speculators that turned into a stampede.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery plummeted 35.35 cents a pound -- nearly 14 percent -- to end at 217.95 cents, the lowest closing price since May 9.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, improving crop weather in the Midwest also served to keep pressure on grain prices.
Soybeans for November delivery closed 12 cents a bushel lower at $6.67 and December delivery corn fell 2-1/2 cents to $2.55-1/2, reflecting the better prospects for big crops at the autumn harvest.

Rumours of buying interest from China, however, kept nearby prices for soybeans firm. July delivery soybeans ended 2 cents a bushel higher at $8.13 and July soybean meal closed up $1.90 a ton at $266.70.

Wheat for July delivery closed down 4-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.63 as a crop tour of eastern Midwest wheat fields reported disease-free, healthy stands of winter wheat. The crop will be harvested next month.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed up 52.9 points at 4,739.6, breaking the previous closing and intraday peaks set May 16. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average climbed 308.73 points, or 1.53 percent, to close at 20,532.55.
